newsitem.title: USA: New photo system a marketing success.
newsitem.headline: New photo system a marketing success.

text.p: Since its April introduction by the world's five largest camera makers, sales of the Advanced Photo System have skyrocketed.
Consumer demand has been so strong that it has outstripped supply, the producers say, and most marketing and advertising efforts have been put aside until they come into balance.
Complicating matters, a second-generation of newer APS cameras is due only months after the debut.

The film-and-camera innovation makes picture-taking easier and provides better print quality because of its silver-based film, manufacturers say. The camera features no-error drop-in loading and a built-in option to select different print sizes on the same roll of film.
Retailers confirms the public has reponded to APS in a very big way.
"Very hot category," says a spokesman for the Willoughby Peerless Camera Stores in Manhattan. "We have trouble keeping up with the demand for the hottest sellers."
A spokeswoman for the 120-store Genovese Drug Store chain on Long Island said, "The APS is very strong for a new system."
Now, the industry-wide marketing for the APS system of cameras and film is entering its new phase aimed at the back-to-school and forthcoming holiday season.
The goal is to achieve the expected 1996 sales of between 2 million and 3 million APS cameras for an average outlay of about $200 each.

Fuji Photo Film USA Inc., based in Elmsford, N.Y., will concentrate on telling the consumer the operating and development features of the new cameras, said Manny Almeda, vice president of marketing for consumer products.

"The main goal, of course, is the big season in the final quarter of the year." Fuji will continue its theme for the APS products of "Smart Cameras. Smart Film. Smart Development. Smart Mini-Labs," he said.
Eastman Kodak Co., of Rochester, N.Y., which introduced eight models, won't say much about its new marketing phase.
"So far, the consumer response to our new cameras has been fabulous," said Paul Allen, a corporate spokesman. "Our plan is to announce more cameras and more film as we go along."

Despite the ongoing and increasingly bitter trade fight between Kodak, the biggest American producer, and Fuji, the largest Japanese photo products maker, the two firms joined with Nikon Corp., Minolta Corp. and Canon Inc. to offer various versions of the APS concept. Kodak beat the pack by announcing the APS in February.
The move by the big five producers was quickly joined by a host of licensees, now numbering well over 50, including Yashica, Olympic and Vivitar.
Most APS brands are in the middle ranges from Kodak's $100-$120 to Nikon's $199 model.

Retailers say that cameras at high-end of the price scale are moving best. This is seen as a promising factor, since it apparently means that customers are willing to pay more for higher technology, more quality and improved pictures.
"Consumers tell us that they love the way the prints come back," observes Kodak's Allen. "In general, we are getting very positive feedback."

Planning soon to introduce a disposable APS model, Fuji is "running 300 percent over our original sales projections," said Almeda. "The downside is that our supply is considerably behind the demand for all five of our models."
Retailers' enthusiasm for the camera and film is high but it is somewhat tempered by what are perceived to be lacks in the marketing approach.
"The sales pitch to the public will need to be focused better," said the spokeswoman for Genovese Drug Stores. "Lots of people still don't know a lot about the new system.
Surprisingly perhaps, the new camera hasn't appreciably hurt sales of the standard 35-mm, single-lens reflex models and film which have been standard fare for years.

Asked why this was the case, Almeda of Fuji replied, "Yes, the new system hasn't hurt our regular 35-mm camera and film. I guess the reason is that the regular 35-mm has evolved into the mainstay for both amateurs and professionals over such a long period that it has a deeply entrenched loyalty."

Obviously, it will all come down to sharply pointed marketing. With a new technology priced at approximately the same levels as the old technology, the boons of the former will have to be and depicted in ways to make the latter seem obsolete. But it shouldn't be too difficult.
Everyone agrees -- the camera business has been treading water for some time now. The APS system has created a lot of new ripples.
